summary: Customer interview transcript with the operations director at Metro Fresh, a regional grocery distributor running 120–200 daily deliveries. Rich source for behavioral alternatives (spreadsheet dispatch), ICP role and trigger, and proof claims. Primary signal for competitive alternatives and audience framing.
key_quotes: Before FixtureCo we were just throwing it together in spreadsheets every morning — one dispatcher, sixty routes, total chaos.
Half our customers had just given up on the same-day promise. We were that bad.
The dispatchers are the ones who own this. If they don't trust the routing, they override it, and then you've lost everything.
We looked at DispatchTrack but it felt like it was built for enterprise fleets, not for a 12-person ops team.
We're not trying to be Amazon. We're trying to not lose the wholesale contracts we already have.

competitors.name: DispatchTrack
competitors.role: evaluated but rejected — perceived as enterprise-only

claims: Wholesale contract retention was primary success metric

summary: Founder-authored narrative document framing FixtureCo's positioning against the manual-coordination status quo. Establishes market category as 'last-mile delivery intelligence' distinct from generic route optimization. Key source for Component 3 (value), Component 4 (ICP), and Component 5 (market category).
key_quotes: The problem isn't that there's no routing software. It's that none of it was built for the dispatcher who also handles customer calls.
Our customers win on reliability, not on speed. That's the category we're in: predictable last-mile, not fast last-mile.
The real alternative is not DispatchTrack or Onfleet. The real alternative is the whiteboard and the group text.
When we say 50–500 deliveries, we mean the band where automation starts paying but enterprise software is still overkill.
A 3PL coordinator managing 8 clients doesn't have time to run a routing algorithm. They need a system that thinks for them.

claims: Automation ROI threshold starts at this scale
